payload.description:
## The defect

`basicly loop supervise` refused to seed any lane from a root whose children are already decomposed, because the **root** carries an unapproved decompose checkpoint, and it did so while a live L3 grant covered that root.

The consequence is the one that matters for throughput: the whole point of supervise is to fan out, and here it fanned out over nothing and returned non zero, forcing a human to hand drive `loop run` once per child. The engine knows the ready set; the driver should not have to.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Issue an L3 grant on an epic that already has open decomposed children: `basicly policy grant <epic> --level L3 --token-budget 80000000 --confirm <code>`. Confirm it reports ISSUED and the bead count it covers.
2. Run `basicly loop supervise <epic> --max-passes 2 --autonomy L3`.
3. Observe the session start, the budget line, and `children: 14 total, 12 open`.
4. Observe `routed: <epic> -> seed-blocked - no lane could be provisioned from 12 open child(ren) - decompose checkpoint awaiting human approval`, then `blocked: no ready lanes and nothing to land`, exit 1.
5. Run `basicly loop run <one open child> --work-type <type> --root <epic> --autonomy L3` and observe the classify checkpoint approved and delegated under the L3 grant on the very same root.

Observed 2026-08-19 on `basicly-rn0o` with a live L3 grant covering 16 beads: supervise seeded nothing, while a per child `loop run` under the same root and the same grant delegated its checkpoint without a human.

Expected: either supervise approves the root decompose checkpoint under the covering grant and seeds the ready children, or it refuses with the reason a grant cannot cover it, so the operator learns which.

## Why this looks like a defect rather than a design choice

`policy.PROPOSAL_COVERAGE` grants L3 the `children` proposal kind, and the comment above it states the ladder is drawn one level stricter for production than for approval, so **L1 may approve a decompose checkpoint** and only origination is restricted to L2 and above. Under that rule an L3 grant should both originate and approve here. Nothing in the refusal names a policy that overrides it.

**Not established:** whether a root whose children already exist takes a different path that never consults the grant, and whether the refusal comes from the seeding code or from the checkpoint evaluation. The record does not guess between them.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a root with open decomposed children and a covering grant at or above the level that may approve a decompose checkpoint when supervise runs then it approves the checkpoint under the grant and seeds the ready children.
- Given the same root with no covering grant when supervise runs then it refuses and names the checkpoint and the level that would cover it.
- Given a grant that genuinely may not cover the checkpoint when supervise refuses then the message names the policy that forbids it rather than saying awaiting human approval.
- Given a seeded fan out then the per child path and the supervise path resolve the same checkpoint the same way.
- Demonstrated by: supervise on an epic with a live L3 grant provisioning at least one lane, against a control run with the grant revoked that refuses and names the level.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `tests/`
payload.title: supervise seeds nothing when a root decompose checkpoint is unapproved even under a live L3 grant

payload.description:
## The defect

Every `basicly loop run` commits tracker state in the **base checkout** before it provisions a worktree, with the message recording the claim before provisioning. Four lanes dispatched in the same second all reached that commit together. One won and three failed, two with exit 1 and one with exit 128, and each returned non zero having done nothing.

So the fan out width of the factory is bounded by a serial step in the base checkout, not by worktree isolation. That is the opposite of what the isolation model advertises, and it is silent: the failure text names a git commit, not contention, so an operator reads it as a hook rejection.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ensure a covering grant is live and four ready records have a complete definition of ready and disjoint scopes.
2. Dispatch all four with `basicly loop run <id> --autonomy L3` within the same second, each in its own background shell.
3. Observe one commit lands, recording the claim before provisioning.
4. Observe the other three exit non zero with `Error: command failed (1)` or `(128)` naming that same git commit.
5. Observe no worktree was provisioned for the three, and no lane state advanced.

Observed 2026-08-19: four lanes dispatched together, one provisioned, three lost. No index lock file remained afterwards and the stash list was empty, so the residue is not what fails; the race is.

Expected: a lane that cannot take the base checkout waits and retries, or the dispatch path serialises on the same lock the ledger already has, and either way the operator learns it was contention.

## Why the supervisor is not already the answer

`basicly loop supervise` exists to serialise a fan out and does hold a session lock. It is not reachable for this case today: on a root whose children are already decomposed it answers seed blocked, no lane could be provisioned, decompose checkpoint awaiting human approval, even under a live L3 grant that policy says may approve it. That is filed as basicly-kjc5.62. So an operator who wants width is pushed to concurrent `loop run`, which is the path that races.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given four ready lanes with disjoint scopes dispatched together when each reaches the base checkout commit then all four eventually provision, or the ones that cannot say they are waiting on contention.
- Given a lane that fails to commit tracker state when it reports the failure then the message names contention rather than naming a git command.
- Given a lane that lost the race when it retries then it does not duplicate the claim it already recorded.
- Given a single lane dispatched alone when it provisions then its behaviour is unchanged.
- Demonstrated by: four concurrent dispatches all reaching a provisioned worktree, against a control run before the fix that loses three

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

payload.description:
## The defect

The scope collision gate refuses a lane that touched a path outside its declared scope. Two of the paths it refuses are files **every lane is expected to write**:

- `basicly.d/<record-id>.toml`, the ratchet rebaseline drop in, which a lane must write in the same commit as the file it pins.
- `changelog.d/<record-id>.<category>.md`, the release note fragment, which the changelog convention says a lane writes instead of editing the assembled file.

Neither is implicitly in scope, so a lane that follows both conventions is refused unless its author remembered to declare two paths whose names are derived from the record id the engine already knows.

Observed 2026-08-19 on `basicly-gvlpxm`: the lane did the right thing, wrote its own drop in and its own fragment, and the gate listed both as out of scope alongside a genuine collision. The genuine finding was buried among two false ones.

## Why the false positives matter more than they look

The message that carries them also carries the real collision, and it ends by offering `[policy] scope_collision = "warn"` as the way to land. An operator who sees two obviously wrong entries in a list of five learns to distrust the list, and the cheapest way to act on that distrust is the setting the message just named. So a false positive here trains an operator to weaken the gate.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a record whose declared scope names only source and test files.
2. Dispatch it. Let the lane write a rebaseline drop in named after the record, and a changelog fragment named after the record.
3. Advance to land. Observe the gate lists both files as outside the declared scope.
4. Observe the record id in each filename matches the lane being landed, so the engine could have derived both.

Observed: two paths derived from the lane own id are reported as scope violations.
Expected: a path whose name is derived from the lane own record id is in scope by construction, and never reported.

## The narrow fix, and what it must not become

Admit exactly two derived paths per lane: the drop in for its own id and the fragments for its own id. **Do not** admit the two directories wholesale, because one lane writing another lane drop in is a real collision and this is the only place it would be caught.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane that writes a drop in named after its own record when the scope gate runs then the file is admitted and not reported.
- Given a lane that writes a changelog fragment named after its own record when the scope gate runs then the file is admitted and not reported.
- Given a lane that writes a drop in named after a different record when the scope gate runs then it is still reported as a violation.
- Given a lane with a genuine collision plus the two derived files when the gate reports then the report names the collision alone.
- Demonstrated by: a landing whose lane wrote both derived files and one genuine out of scope edit, where the report names exactly one path

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_merge_scope.py`

payload.description:
## Problem

A session with no grant has **no spend ceiling of any kind**, and now that the supervisor can seed
its own lanes it will happily dispatch metered agents under exactly that condition.

Both halves of D3's ceiling are keyed on the grant. `policy.spend_status` returns
`halted=False` outright when `grant is None or grant.token_budget is None`, and
`SpendStatus.remaining_tokens` returns `None` for the same case, which makes
`policy.check_pass_spend` return `None` — admitted. So an ungranted `basicly loop supervise <root>`
passes both the retrospective and the forward gate unconditionally and dispatches up to
`[worktree] concurrency` headless agents with no bound.

This was latent while `loop supervise` could not start work on a cold root: an operator had to
provision lanes by hand, which meant they were already deciding to spend. basicly-t73d removed that
step, so the hazard is now one command deep — and `[runner] default` is no longer `manual`
(basicly-euyt), so that command dispatches real agents. Observed while exercising t73d: with
basicly-jr0l's grant revoked, a supervise pass provisioned three worktrees and would have dispatched
into them; nothing was spent only because the run was interrupted.

The authorization argument matters as much as the arithmetic. A grant is the one human confirm that
authorizes delegated spend. Dispatching a metered runner with no grant spends money that nobody
approved and that no ceiling bounds.

## Steps to Reproduce

```sh
uv run basicly policy grant <root> --revoke
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import policy
s = policy.spend_status(Path('.'), '<root>')
print('grant', s.grant, 'halted', s.halted, 'remaining', s.remaining_tokens)
print('forward verdict:', policy.check_pass_spend(10**9, s))
"
```

Observed - `grant None halted False remaining None`, and the forward verdict is `None` for a
forecast of a billion tokens, i.e. admitted. A supervise pass on that root then provisions and
dispatches.

Expected - a **metered** dispatch requires a covering grant with a token budget; without one the
pass refuses and says so, and the refusal is surfaced the way the other spend refusals are. A
handoff runner is unaffected, because it spends nothing.

## Scope

- src/basicly/supervise.py
- src/basicly/policy.py
- tests/test_supervise.py
- tests/test_policy.py

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a session whose root carries no grant with a token budget when a supervised pass would
  dispatch a metered headless runner then it dispatches nothing and reports that a covering grant is
  required, while a handoff runner still proceeds because it spends nothing
payload.title: A session with no grant has no spend ceiling yet still dispatches metered agents

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-08-20 while landing the absent record guard for `basicly-6oypkd`. That guard sits in
`owned_write.append`, which every engine write reaches through `tracker.write` or `tracker.try_write`.

`tracker.add_artifact` does not. It is a seventh write path that bypasses `owned_write` entirely and
still accepts an artifact for a record the ledger does not hold. So the guard covers six verbs and one
surface sits outside it, which is the shape where a control reads as complete and is not.

This is a live hole rather than a theoretical one: an artifact is how a loop state hands the next one its
evidence, so an artifact filed against a mistyped id is evidence attached to nothing, and the state that
needed it reads as carrying none.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Seed a temp repo with the kit installed and one known record.
2. Call `tracker.add_artifact` for a record id the ledger does not hold.
3. Observe an artifact event is appended and no refusal is raised.
4. Call the same for the seeded record and observe it appended too, which is the positive control.
5. Call any of the six guarded verbs for the absent id and observe a refusal, so the inconsistency is between surfaces rather than in the guard.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an artifact recorded against a record the ledger does not hold then the write is refused naming the id - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_mirror.py -k artifact_absent -q`
- Given an artifact recorded against a held record then it is appended unchanged and content deduplication still applies

## Scope

- `src/basicly/tracker.py`
- `tests/test_mirror.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/tracker.py`
- `tests/test_mirror.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest -q`

Mutation removing the guard call fails the named check. Full verify PASS, 31 checks, 4473 tests.

Correction to this record's stated consequence. It says an artifact against a mistyped id is evidence attached to nothing. Measured: the fold DOES mint the id, as a record with no created event, so ledger-bodies reports it at the next commit - I reproduced that directly, 'records: 1 bodyless: (proj-ghost,)'. The hole was covered downstream. Refusing at the seam is still right because an append-only log has no undelete and the event is already written by the time that gate speaks, but the record overstated it.

26 existing tests depended on the tolerance, across test_artifact_record, test_handoff and test_handoff_states, each writing an artifact against a record its fixture never created. All fixed by opening the record, the way 6oypkd fixed the same shape in test_gate_source._repo. The two autouse fixtures key off request.fixturenames rather than taking work_repo, so the tracked-tree copy is not built for the tests that only want tmp_path.

Deviations from the declared scope, all forced. The test went to tests/test_artifact_record.py, not tests/test_mirror.py which the acceptance check names: test_mirror.py is rebaselined at exactly 4048 with zero headroom. I measured every candidate first - test_owned_write 290, test_tracker_seam 141, test_artifact_record 1351. The -k artifact_absent selector is preserved; my first test name missed it and pytest exited 5, which is the failure 6oypkd's own fragment predicted for this shape. test_gate_source.py's docstring cited the private symbol name and was repointed.

The blocker, and it is the finding. tests/test_handoff.py needed 190 tokens against a frozen 6302, having already been rebaselined three times: 3986 to 4134 (pp7q4i), to 5124 (gvlpxm), to 6302 (u2hl.59). Plus 58 percent, three fragments, one reason each time, and all three deferred the same extraction. That extraction has landed - cut_violation is in artifact_record now. The test-side home they named, test_handoff_schemas.py, has 2158 tokens of room and is the wrong responsibility: it validates schema files, takes no repo fixture and never calls handoff.record. They justified deferral on room, not on fit. Recorded on basicly-8ro0nx and basicly-wpqdag.

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-08-22 while labelling a record for a supervised pass. The write reported `recorded:` and the field did not change. Three commands in a row reported success and wrote nothing:

```text
tracker write -- update basicly-fi1i7z --add-label live-demo   -> recorded:   labels stayed ''
tracker write -- update basicly-fi1i7z --labels    live-demo   -> recorded:   labels stayed ''
tracker write -- update basicly-fi1i7z --labels    live-pass-2 -> recorded:   labels became 'live-pass-2'
```

The events on the record explain it:

```text
field {"name":"labels","value":"live-demo"}     the first add
field {"name":"labels","value":""}              the remove
                                                 the second add: no event at all
```

## The cause is documented and this is it biting

Architecture 32.2: *"The id is a digest over the kind, the payload and the generation. It deliberately excludes the timestamp. A replay of the same logical write is therefore idempotent. The trap that buys is documented, not hidden: a re-record of an identical fact is swallowed, so a genuine reopen needs a new generation."*

So **an add, then a remove, then the same add again is permanently stuck at removed.** The third write is byte-identical to the first, its digest already exists, and it is swallowed. The fold takes the last event in canonical order, which is the removal.

This is not specific to labels. Any field driven to value A, then to B, then back to A has the same shape, and so does a close then reopen then close.

## Why it costs more than a re-typed command

The seam prints `recorded:`. Nothing distinguishes *appended* from *already had this exact event*, so a caller reads success and moves on. It cost three commands and a wrong diagnosis here; on a status field it would leave a record in a state the operator believes they changed.

## The generation exists and nothing reaches it

`events.event_id_for` takes a generation precisely so a genuine re-record can be distinguished. No write verb exposes it, so a caller has no way to say "yes, again, on purpose".

## Acceptance Criteria

- WHEN a write produces an event whose id the ledger already holds, THE SEAM SHALL say so rather than printing `recorded:`.
- WHEN a caller means the re-record genuinely, THERE SHALL be a way to say so, and the resulting event SHALL fold to the intended value.
- WHEN a field is driven A then B then A, THE FOLDED VALUE SHALL be A.
- WHERE the swallow is correct - a true duplicate replay - THE BEHAVIOUR SHALL NOT change, because idempotent replay is the property the digest exists for.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/owned_write.py`
- `src/basicly/write_verbs.py`
- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py`
- `tests/test_owned_write.py`

## Plan

- integrity: `L3`
- budget: `110000`
- depends on: none
- demonstration: Drive one field A then B then A and read back A, against a control that replays one identical write twice and appends once.

{"detail": "AC1 and AC4 are landed and verified in commit 79bbe0db (seam now prints 'already recorded, so nothing was appended'; 4787 passed; ruff, module-size and comment-density green; demonstrated on the bead's exact CLI sequence). AC2/AC3 are not done.

What I tried, and why it is a requirements question rather than a coding one. I implemented the bead's implied fix in .basicly/core/kit/tracker/events.py: treat a colliding event id as a replay only when the record already states the fact, else walk Draft.generation to a free id. It passes the bead's demonstration exactly - labels A->B->A folds to A, status closed->open->closed folds to closed, and a single identical write still appends once. It is still wrong. Two tests pin the opposite on purpose: test_replaying_the_same_drafts_appends_nothing re-appends 3 events under such a rule, and test_a_repeated_status_needs_a_generation_or_it_is_swallowed asserts the swallow 'in both directions' as a documented property. The reason is not a fixable detail: replaying the history 'A, B' and deliberately re-recording 'A' after 'B' leave the ledger byte-identical, so no fact in it separates them. AC3 and AC4 are jointly unsatisfiable for any implicit rule. The refuted patch and the written-up finding are in .basicly/usage/scratch/refuted-state-based-replay.patch and .basicly/usage/scratch/finding-ac3-is-unachievable-implicitly.md.

The second, independent blocker is measured headroom. The declared scope has 120 tokens of total room (owned_write.py 36, write_verbs.py 13, events.py 0, tests/test_owned_write.py 71) against roughly 600 needed; I landed AC1 by putting the seam report in tracker_write.py and the test in tests/test_tracker_write.py, both of which have room and are the correct homes, but neither is in the declared scope. Fitting AC2 needs either room freed in owned_write.py/write_verbs.py, or an authorised extraction: the six private cap helpers in events.py (_truncate, _redacted, _text_bound, _text_size, _refuse_unbounded, _prepare_entry, 1749 tokens) have zero code references outside that file and would move cleanly, but that is a new deployed kit module and a decomposition track the module-size gate itself disclaims as this change's obligation. I did not use a waiver: check_module_size._module_finding shows a waiver replaces the frozen entry outright, so waiving events.py would delete its 15041-token ceiling and license unbounded growth in exchange for 465 tokens.

What would unblock me: 'implement --again in <module>' or 'authorise the events.py cap-helper extraction' or 'AC1 is sufficient, close the rest'.", "question": "AC2/AC3 of basicly-kn4rip need a decision I cannot take: (a) is AC3 ('a field driven A then B then A SHALL fold to A') to be satisfied only through AC2's explicit affordance - a `--again` flag on the write surface that bumps Draft.generation - given that an implicit state-based rule is refuted by the existing suite? and (b) if yes, which module absorbs it, because every file in the bead's declared scope is at its module-size ratchet: write_verbs.py has 13 tokens of headroom and owned_write.py has 4, against the ~30-40 the flag needs."}

{"answer": "AC1 is sufficient for this record. Close it on what it verified and land 79bbe0db. Owner decision 2026-08-22.

Your refutation is accepted and is the reason: replaying the history A,B and deliberately re-recording A after B leave the ledger byte-identical, so no implicit rule can separate them, and AC3 and AC4 are jointly unsatisfiable for any such rule. That is a finding, not a failure to deliver.

AC2 and AC3 are already filed as basicly-z9bggw, which blocks on this record. It carries the mechanism with line references, a scratch-ledger proof that generation=2 lands the same fact and moves the fold, a verb-by-verb table of where A-then-B-then-A is reachable, and the constraint that decides the design: tracker.scrub_ledger re-derives every generation as the dense occurrence count on the commit path and raises TrackerDivergenceError if any id fails to re-mint, so the flag must resolve to occurrence_count + 1 rather than mint arbitrarily. Its scope is owned_write.py, tracker_argv.py and tracker_write.py, which have room; the strip belongs in owned_write.append beside _resolve_labels, after _stamped, because that is the one place holding the ledger lock a dense-occurrence resolver needs.

Do NOT extract the events.py cap helpers for this. Your reading is right and is the reason: a waiver replaces the frozen entry outright, so waiving events.py would delete its 15041-token ceiling to buy 465 tokens. Separately, the waiver guidance you were given is itself wrong - the python-guidelines skill prescribes a format the gate refuses and never mentions rebaselining, which is the permitted route. That is filed as basicly-03ykuf.

Two further defects your probing surfaced are filed as basicly-wu4w8v: the kit CLI raises IndexError at cli.py:322 when every draft is swallowed, and verify.py:415 and rubrics.py:536 discard the boolean you added and report a swallowed gate as recorded."}
